sections.section_title: Clinical Presentation, Differential, and Initial Evaluation of Failed Transcatheter Aortic Valves After Treated PVE
sections.description: Uses the case to frame how to assess symptomatic deterioration of a prior TAVI—especially in a patient with a history of prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE)—and to distinguish structural valve issues from active infection or other causes.
key_points: Common presentations: exertional dyspnoea, chest discomfort, dizziness, heart failure signs; review comorbidities (CAD, COPD, diabetes, conduction disease) and prior valve history.

Differential diagnosis of post-TAVI dysfunction: structural valve deterioration (SVD), prosthesis thrombosis, pannus/underexpansion, leaflet immobility after prior endocarditis, paravalvular leak, patient–prosthesis mismatch (PPM), and recurrent/ongoing PVE.

Rule out active PVE before reintervention: repeat blood cultures, inflammatory markers, transthoracic/TEE for vegetations or abscess, and CT for perivalvular complications; consider PET/CT if equivocal.
Hemodynamic assessment: quantify stenosis/regurgitation with TTE (mean gradient, AVA by continuity equation, indexed AVA, Doppler velocity index; DVI <0.25 suggests severe stenosis/PPM).
Risk stratification for reintervention: surgical risk (e.g., EuroSCORE II), anatomical feasibility, prior frame integration, bleeding history, coronary disease and need for future access.
Guideline perspective: surgery is preferred for active/complicated PVE; once infection is eradicated, reintervention strategy should be individualized by a multidisciplinary heart team.

sections.section_title: Pathophysiology: SVD, Sequelae of Endocarditis, and PPM Across Serial TAVI
sections.description: Explains mechanisms of failure in transcatheter bioprostheses and how prior endocarditis and layered frames affect leaflet motion, gradients, and orifice area.
key_points: SVD mechanisms: leaflet calcification/fibrosis, stent underexpansion, leaflet pinwheeling or inward folding after prior VIV, and cumulative frame constraint in serial implants.
Endocarditis effects: leaflet injury and scarring with mechanical restriction; once cured, residual leaflet damage can accelerate SVD without active infection.
PPM in VIV/TAV-in-TAV-in-TAV: reduced effective orifice area from supra-annular leaflet stacking and reduced expansion; identify by elevated gradients, small indexed AVA, low DVI.
Immediate post-implant high gradients may reflect underexpansion and transient hemodynamics; subsequent reduction can occur with remodeling and further frame expansion after post-dilation.
Trade-offs in serial TAVI: maintaining coronary patency and future access versus maximizing EOA; commissural alignment and implantation height influence both.

sections.section_title: Multimodality Imaging and Preprocedural Planning for TAV-in-TAV-in-TAV
sections.description: Details CT- and echo-guided planning steps that determine feasibility, device selection, implantation depth, and coronary protection strategy in triple-layered frames.
key_points: CT measurements: inner lumen diameter of the in-situ frame(s), annular and sinus dimensions, coronary ostial heights, valve-to-coronary (VTC) distance, valve-to-sinotubular junction distance, sinus width/height.

Risk of coronary obstruction/sinus sequestration: short VTC (<3–4 mm) or narrow sinuses, tall leaflets, and layered frames increase risk; evaluate potential neo-skirt height relative to coronary ostia.
Commissural alignment planning: preprocedural modeling to align new valve commissures with prior frame leaflets to preserve coronary windows and maximize EOA.
Valve choice and sizing: use CT-derived internal diameters of the most restrictive frame; consider supra-annular, lower-frame, alignment-friendly devices in narrow anatomies.

Deciding on protection: criteria for upfront coronary protection (guidewires, chimney stenting) or leaflet modification (e.g., BASILICA) versus proceeding without protection if CT shows adequate clearance.
Access strategy: assess iliofemoral disease and prior access complications; plan adjunct radial access for aortography and coronary monitoring.
Baseline imaging to exclude active infection: TEE and CT to confirm absence of vegetations, abscess, or paravalvular leaks.

sections.section_title: Interventional Strategy: Device Deployment, Gradient Optimization, and Periprocedural Care
sections.description: Outlines stepwise execution of a third TAVI within two prior frames, techniques to minimize PPM and protect coronaries, and immediate post-implant assessment and medical management.
key_points: Procedure steps: establish femoral delivery and radial monitoring access; LV wire placement; rapid pacing; targeted predilation to assess leaflet mobility and confirm coronary patency; controlled deployment with fluoroscopic/CT landmarks.
High implantation rationale: seating the new frame at the level of prior leaflet tips to pin immobile leaflets outward, reduce inward folding, limit neo-skirt height, and preserve coronary flow.
Commissural alignment execution: use device-specific markers to align with prior commissures; aim to maintain coronary reaccess windows through triple meshes.
Gradient reduction: post-dilation with appropriately sized noncompliant balloons to optimize expansion of current and prior frames; avoid uncontrolled fracture unless deliberately planned.
Intra-procedural surveillance: aortography for regurgitation and coronary patency; hemodynamic measurements; TTE/TEE as needed.

Periprocedural considerations: antibiotic prophylaxis given prior PVE; tailor antithrombotic therapy to bleeding and CAD history (often single antiplatelet absent other indications); manage conduction system and existing pacemaker.
Success criteria and complications: apply VARC-3 endpoints; anticipate risks of coronary obstruction, annular/root injury, vascular access complications, stroke, PPM, and leaflet thrombosis.

sections.description: Presents expected hemodynamic trajectory after triple TAVI, surveillance strategies, and planning for future coronary and valve interventions in a lifetime management framework.
key_points: Hemodynamic course: immediate post-implant gradients may be high in constrained anatomies; expect improvement over weeks with frame expansion and LV remodeling if implantation and post-dilation were optimized.
Monitoring: TTE before discharge, at 1–3 months, and at least annually (AVA, mean gradient, DVI, regurgitation, EF); assess symptoms and functional capacity.
Infection prevention: dental hygiene, endocarditis prophylaxis where indicated; maintain high index of suspicion for recurrent infection in febrile episodes.
Antithrombotic strategy: favor the lowest-risk regimen consistent with CAD status and bleeding history; reassess need for DAPT or anticoagulation if new indications arise.
Coronary access after triple frames: document commissural orientation and coronary windows; plan for challenging reaccess and consider CT roadmaps for future PCI.

Future options if failure occurs: limited surgical feasibility; consider valve fracture, high-pressure post-dilation, or leaflet laceration (e.g., BASILICA) in select anatomies, recognizing uncertain safety in triple-stented valves.
Patient-centered care: shared decision-making, heart-team review, and documentation of procedural details to inform future interventions.
